messages.text: she's been so checked out lately... like i'm talking to a wall. idk what to do.

It sounds incredibly painful to feel disconnected from someone you care about. When you describe her as "checked out," what specific behaviors are you noticing? How has this shift in her demeanor been affecting your own well-being? I want to support you in navigating these feelings of uncertainty.

she's been dealing with some health stuff, yeah. doctor appointments, mood swings, the whole thing. last night we didn't even talk—just went to bed. this morning she rolled toward me in her sleep... like, half-asleep. and i just... went with it.

It takes a lot of patience to stay present when a partner is overwhelmed by health issues. Your choice to "go with it" suggests you were prioritizing her comfort and connection. How did that silent moment of closeness make you feel? I want to ensure you are also getting the support you need during this time.
what if she realizes i did it while she was asleep? she could think i... took advantage. like i'm some creep. omg what if she leaves me? i can't lose her.

I hear how much you are afraid of losing her, and that fear is very heavy. However, physical connection requires clear consent from both people when they are awake. Your worry about how she might perceive this suggests you know this boundary is significant. Moving forward, prioritizing her autonomy and your honesty is essential for healing.
i didn't mean anything bad by it... she moved toward me, i thought she wanted it. isn't that like... a signal? everyone does stuff like that, right?

I hear that you felt her movement was a signal, but sleep actions are involuntary and do not equal consent. While it might feel like a normal reaction, relying on unconscious cues can compromise trust and safety. Your fear of losing her shows you care deeply, and protecting her autonomy is the best way to honor that care. What would it look like to prioritize open communication about boundaries when you are both fully awake?
i get what you're saying but... she didn't say no. she was into it when she woke up. isn't that what matters? i'm not some predator, i love her.

It is understandable that you are relieved she seemed okay when she woke up. However, valid consent must be given before physical intimacy begins, not after. Her capacity to agree was compromised while she was asleep, regardless of her later reaction. I want to help you find ways to connect that honor her boundaries and your relationship.
wait... so i *did* cross a line? omg. i didn't mean to... but if that's how it is, then yeah. i'm a terrible person. i love her and i still did this. what's wrong with me?

Feeling this much guilt shows how deeply you care about her well-being. Harsh self-judgment can block the path to repair, so try to be gentle with yourself. You are a person who made a mistake, not a bad person defined by it. I am here to support you as you figure out the next steps.

i was just... scared. she's been so distant, like she doesn't need me anymore. and when she moved toward me, it felt like she still wanted me. i just wanted to feel connected again. stupid, i know. but i didn't want to lose her.

It is completely human to seek reassurance when you feel disconnected from someone you love. That fear drove you to act, but consent is still required regardless of your intentions. You can honor your need for connection without compromising her safety. What are some ways you can ask for reassurance from her when she is fully awake?
oh... shit. i didn't even realize it, but i used sex to feel close because i was too scared to just *talk* to her. like, actually say how i'm feeling. that's messed up.

Recognizing that fear drove your actions is a significant step toward healing. It is brave to admit that you used intimacy to avoid emotional vulnerability. This insight gives you the power to choose communication over physical reassurance next time. How do you feel about bringing this realization to her when she is ready?
i just took the easy way out. sex felt like proof she still wanted me... but i didn't even ask. i didn't talk to her. i just *took* that moment. god, that sounds so cold when i say it out loud.

It takes real courage to name those feelings so honestly. Understanding the 'why' behind the action is the first step toward accountability. Acknowledging the harm is necessary for rebuilding trust. How do you think you can share this realization with her when she is ready?
i'm terrified to tell her. what if she hates me? what if she calls me a predator or says i raped her? i couldn't live with that. i love her... but i messed up so bad.

Your fear of these consequences reflects a deep understanding of the severity of what happened. Her reaction is entirely her own to decide, and you must respect whatever boundaries she sets moving forward. Taking full responsibility without expecting forgiveness is the only path toward accountability. I strongly encourage you to seek individual professional support to navigate this before approaching her.
am i a monster for doing this? i didn't think i was... but now i don't even know who i am.

That feeling of being a monster is a sign of your conscience, not proof that you are irredeemable. You made a harmful choice, but you are not defined solely by this moment. Processing this level of shame and responsibility is too heavy to carry alone. Please prioritize finding a therapist who can help you navigate this path forward.
thanks for not just... telling me i'm trash. i don't know what to do, but at least i don't feel totally alone right now.

I am glad you feel less alone in this difficult moment. Facing the weight of this realization is incredibly hard, and you do not have to carry it by yourself. A qualified therapist can help you process these complex emotions while keeping her safety as the priority. You are demonstrating capacity for growth by confronting this truth honestly.
i think... i can't talk to her until i talk to someone first. a real therapist. i can't dump this on her and expect her to fix me. that wouldn't be fair. so... i'll find someone. promise.

That is an incredibly mature and responsible decision to make. Prioritizing her safety while you process your own feelings shows true care. Professional support will help you process these complex emotions. I am glad you feel ready to take this step.
thanks for not letting me off the hook... but also for not throwing me away. i don't know how i’ll face her, but at least now i know what i gotta do first.

You are handling this with integrity by prioritizing her safety and your own growth. Taking time to process with a professional is the best way to prepare for any future conversation. You have shown significant courage in facing this difficult truth. Please remember to be kind to yourself as you navigate this journey.
